784.s: Queen says the young lions cannot match players who lived the history, such as Sweets and Lockjaw Davis.
784.q: Well they suffer from the hype they get because they really can’t live up to these stages. I mean a man, people like Harry “Sweets” Edison and Lockjaw, this is easily men of caliber who, they got something to talk about. They can give you a book. But a person who’s worked with one or two bands…

784.t: Horace Silver auditions and the loss of real bands
784.s: Queen says Silver tests tempo discipline and that young players lack big-band experience of sounding as one.
784.q: Yeah. America, I love to work here, if the people are looking for what’s correct. My music is not about a challenge. My music is about reality. That’s it. So if they look for a drummer with twenty drums and red lights flashing in there, hey, you know, you’re not going to get the drum from me.…

418.t: Young players coming up: Warren Vache
418.s: Young players should get road experience; he predicts the not-yet-20 Warren Vache will be one of the big ones, and the music's core will remain.
418.q: Yeah. I mean they -- I don't mind it if -- if a young guy can do it -- It's OK for a young guy to do it, you know. He's got his health and everything. And then he can get experience which you do need to be a band musician.

418.t: Young players coming up: Warren Vache
418.s: Young players should get road experience; he predicts the not-yet-20 Warren Vache will be one of the good ones.
418.q: Yes. I think... I don't mind... If a young guy can do it... It's okay for a young guy to do it, you know. Because you've got to have health and everything, and then you get experience, which you do need if you're going to play music.

1051.t: A young St. Augustine band playing old style
1051.s: Mrs. Henderson describes teenage musicians from St. Augustine playing old-style rather than bebop.
1051.q: Me, Harold. So I was dancing. Carol and Codes and Mike Boxer and Amherst Space and I'd trip on them.

706.t: Younger street bands, old man Moret and Jack Teagarden
706.s: He says the young want volume without feeling, recalls Moret's band leading, and tells of jumping on stage with Teagarden after a flight.
706.q: Well, it'll be some down there. But I think they got the wrong idea about things. They want to blow the roof off. All volume and no feeling. Yeah. And then we look around, the chop's tied. Yeah. But in my days coming up, like a man like old man Morett, he was way up in age. See, and there were…

189.s: He admires the young brass bands.
189.q: Well a lot of the older musicians don't like it. But I like it because at least they are playing. And if they play long enough, somebody will get in with them and show them the right way to play, and they'll learn how to read music. And I admire what they're doing.

893.t: The future of New Orleans jazz
893.s: Green and the interviewer discuss young players, recordings and survival of the music.
893.q: Mixed, mixed feelings, Tom. Uh, I think it's such a specialized art form it can get away from you unless you hear it and play it as often as possible. I think the tendency, there is, in any band, there's a tendency for a band to disintegrate, less ensemble and more solo. Uh, all over the world,…

606.t: Young players, unpaid gigs and rising guitarists
606.s: Ellis can't name players imitating him, jokes about never being paid, and names Joe Cohn and John Pizzarelli as good young guitarists.
606.q: I couldn’t name but there are quite a few, you’d be amazed. And that’s really a compliment. I wish I could think of some of them, but it’s hard for me to think of what I had for breakfast this morning.

617.t: Feel that can't be put in a book; young wunderkinds
617.s: Some things can't be written in a book; he praises naturally savvy young players and conferences.
617.q: Yes. I mean to me this is why people even like the music is the way it feels. And so when we start making everything we do be put in a book, I mean I’ve written a book, but there are certain things that I just can’t put in a book because it’s impossible. Forget about it. And some people are looking…

751.t: Integrity, gatekeepers and players recording tracks at home
751.s: Asked about 'integrity', Rowe says there are fewer gatekeepers, so young players should have their work vetted before releasing it online.
751.q: Um hum. Yeah. It’s definitely a shift. I’ve been hearing that more and more from players, that that’s a big part of what they do now. And yeah, I mean I think in order to be one of those players that’s going to have those tracks sent to them, like a Randy Brecker or Marshall Gilkes or whoever it…

906.t: Future of jazz: young talent and college bands
906.s: She names Roy Hargrove, an a cappella group in Seattle, and the UNLV jazz orchestra as signs of hope.
906.q: And Joe goes ‘round to colleges and universities, and he is enormously heartened by the music and the sound, and we were in Seattle where they have a choral group with no music, whatever you call that.

477.t: Jazz education's growth, speed and the lack of communication
477.s: They discuss the disconnect between jazz education and sales, and players focusing on exercises and fast playing.
477.q: I agree. You know the music is getting so fast. It reflects the society we live in today. I mean you can do everything instantly rather than develop an emotion. People don’t have time. They don’t want to wait for the story and the conclusion, they just want to hear the conclusion. Oh my God. And…

153.s: He thinks jazz is healthy, names young players, and recalls Duke saying jazz is beyond category.
153.q: I think that jazz today is good. It’s good. The young players, like the college students – I could name some college bands that are fantastic. They can take my whole book, and they’ll play it. A lot of the young players, like Nicholas Payton, trumpet player – if Louis Armstrong were living, he’d…

417.t: Advice and encouragement for Mark Whitfield and Russell Malone
417.s: Benson praises younger guitarists and says he left them on their right path.
417.q: Definitely. I love that young fellow. I heard him in his budding years, when he first came to New York and he was part of what they called the Young Lions. He lived up to those things. I think he has some ways to go. I think some things, some realizations, and need a producer and a manager who…

368.t: State of jazz today and clarinetists he follows
368.s: He thinks jazz is healthy and names Anat Cohen, Paquito D'Rivera and others.
368.q: It’s in pretty fairly healthy condition by comparison, say by comparing twenty or thirty years ago, it was almost nonexistent, almost. But there again, all those band directors through the years that kept at the big band and jazz as an important part of our lives and as an American art form helped…

86.t: No resentment of young players being signed
86.s: He says he does not resent youngsters' success.
86.ch: Style, originality and the younger generation
86.q: No, I don’t resent it. I never have been resentment of nobody who’s successful. But I do think they should make an allowance for anybody that’s got the talent whether they’re young or old. ‘Cause I hear some of these youngsters can’t play near as good as some of these old-timers.

527.t: Opinion of young players: technician versus artist
527.s: Young players are proficient; jazz requires living experience and individuality.
527.q: [44:35] Like I said, they’re all playing. There’s all these guys I hear. I don’t hear nobody that sounds bad. I’m sure there must be somebody that sound bad, I just don’t get to hear them, but the ones I hear, it’s just a matter of living long enough to have some experience of life that you can put…

451.q: Oh, yeah. Julian Lage. Yeah, he’s, he’s really something. He’s… I met him when he was eleven out in California at Yoshi’s. He came in with his parents. And just for the heck of it, we went in the dressing room and he played my guitar. He sounded fantastic when he was eleven. And I’d been hearing…

108.s: Marsalis's musicians are educated, dedicated and clean-cut.
108.ch: Style, the future of jazz and later playing
108.q: I’ll tell you. These musicians, all of them with this orchestra, were – they were very high-class people, well educated and very dedicated. They have a tremendous awareness of who they are and how they’re being judged by people who come to see them, pay to hear the orchestra play. It’s quite nice.…

464.t: Young musicians, technique versus emotion, and his current projects
464.s: He praises young players' skills but says technique should serve expression, and lists his present workshops and State Department experiences.
464.q: Well, as I look forward I’m seeing a number of very, very accomplished musicians come on the scene, on every instrument. At ages that are less than 25, their skill levels are unbelievable. That they have taken what the older masters have done and learned how to do that, and are able to do that and…

426.t: Recording young musicians such as Christian Scott without judging
426.s: Rudy tries to give young groups what they want, praising a Christian Scott session.
426.q: Of course, well I remember my fundamental laws of existence, its not me to make judgments. When they come in here, and I think I’m good at that, I know what they’re trying to do and I try to give them what they’re trying to do. That’s part of what I do. I don’t see any problem, any being judgmental…

614.t: No deficits in the current generation of players
614.s: The current young musicians are socially conscious, communicate well and mature on the road, with none of the old silent groups.
614.q: And I'll tell you why. For instance, socially and in other ways, this most modern breed are one of the grooviest groups I've ever worked with, as far as just basic people.

97.t: Young players lack training; big bands return
97.q: Oh, there are quite a few of them, quite a few of them, yes. Quite a few. But they haven't got the same interest in music. As soon as -- well, I'll tell you what happened at the Amsterdam one time. There was a woman there that -- of course, we have women that are members now, they're musicians. And…

78.t: Young players can't read or play 'Stardust'; creators versus imitators
78.s: Horace laments that young musicians cannot play standard melodies or verses, losing their tone when reading, and says the old players were creators while many today imitate.
78.ch: Arranging for Fletcher, Goodman and Barnet
78.q: That's the truth. So I don't know whether this hurt the guys or not, you know, musicians. I'm not gonna quote on that, but I'll tell you one thing, though, while we're talking about the musicians. The younger guys, with all due respect to them, I know having been here in Denver and a few other…
